issues.legal_issue: When a party sued in a representative capacity dies during a pending appeal and the interest in the subject matter passes to a successor, the appeal is governed by the rule for devolution of interest rather than the rules for substitution of legal representatives on death.
material_facts: The suit sought possession and management of a religious institution and its properties, with the plaintiff claiming to be its de jure head and the defendant being sued as its de facto head.
The defendant died while the plaintiff’s appeal was pending, and a successor was elected as the institution’s head.
The application to implead the successor was made after the period prescribed for an application under the rules concerning legal representatives.
issues.conclusion: The interest in the subject matter devolved on the successor, so the appeal could be continued against him under Order 22, rule 10, with the court’s leave; it did not abate merely because the application was late under Order 22, rules 3 or 4.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order 22, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure, where a person is sued in a representative capacity and that person’s interest in the subject matter devolves on another, the proceeding may be continued against the person acquiring the interest with the court’s leave. This applies whether the devolution results from death or another event. The Court relied on and approved Rajnam Pillai v. Natraja Desikar, Thirumalai v. Arunachella, and Roshan Lal v. Kapur Chand.

predicates.civil_appeal_pending: An appeal concerning the disputed subject matter was pending when the relevant party died.
predicates.representative_capacity_case: A party was sued in a representative role concerning the subject matter, rather than in a personal capacity.
predicates.subject_matter_interest_devolved_to_succ: The interest of the deceased party in the disputed subject matter passed to a successor.

issues.definition: When an appeal is pending in a representative-capacity case and the deceased party’s interest in the subject matter passes to a successor, the appeal may continue against that successor with the court’s leave.

issues.legal_issue: Uncertainty about who will succeed to a representative office at the time of a party’s death does not prevent devolution of the party’s interest when a successor is later elected to that office.
material_facts: The defendant was sued as the de facto head of an institution and did not claim the institution or its properties adversely to it.
The identity of the next head was uncertain when the defendant died, and the successor was elected afterward.
The suit concerned possession and management of the institution and its properties, and the successor obtained the defendant’s interest in that subject matter by virtue of the election.
issues.conclusion: Devolution occurred when the successor was elected; the uncertainty at the time of death did not prevent the appeal from being continued against the successor under Order 22, rule 10.
issues.legal_principle: Order 22, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure applies when an interest in the subject matter devolves during a pending proceeding. In a representative-capacity case, the interest may devolve when a successor is elected after the former officeholder’s death; the successor need not have been identifiable at the time of death. The Court relied on and approved Rajnam Pillai v. Natraja Desikar, Thirumalai v. Arunachella, and Roshan Lal v. Kapur Chand.
